w: A peak in the Western Tatras straddling the Slovak border, Kasprowy Wierch has been one of Poland's flagship winter ski areas for decades. A cable car runs up daily, putting the summit within easy reach outside ski season too, while the ridge still draws hikers willing to walk it in fair weather.
s: Poland's main ski peak, reached daily by cable car
_facts: Peak of a long crest in the Western Tatras, one of Poland's main ski areas
Southern crests mark the border with Slovakia
Accessible by foot in most conditions, daily by cablecar

w: Rising to 1,894 metres, Great Giewont is among the tallest Western Tatra peaks entirely within Poland, and its ridge has become the visual shorthand for Zakopane, the Tatras and the whole Podhale region. Generations of legends, poems and paintings have been built around this one massif.
s: The peak that symbolizes Zakopane and the Tatras
_facts: Great Giewont peak is 1,894m, among the highest Western Tatra peaks entirely in Poland
Regarded as the symbol of Zakopane, the Polish Tatras and Podhale
Subject of many legends, poems and works of art

w: A funicular has hauled visitors up Gubalowka since 1938, one of the oldest mechanized ascents in the Tatras and still the easiest route to a panorama over Zakopane and the mountains beyond. A chairlift to neighboring Butorowy Wierch followed in 1978 - no climbing required, just a short ride.
s: Funicular-topped hill with the classic Zakopane view
_facts: Gubalowka Hill funicular opened 1938, connecting Zakopane to the summit
Chair lift to Butorowy Wierch opened 1978
Popular tourist attraction with commanding views of the Tatras and Zakopane

w: Opened in 1925 on Krokiew mountain, the Wielka Krokiew ski jump has hosted three FIS Nordic World Championships and remains a fixture of the modern World Cup circuit, especially since local hero Adam Malysz made it one of the sport's best-attended venues. In 1997 Pope John Paul II said mass at its stadium.
s: Ski jump hill where Pope John Paul II said mass
_facts: Biggest ski jumping hill in Zakopane, opened 1925, capacity 40,001
Hosted 1929, 1939 and 1962 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships
Pope John Paul II celebrated mass at the stadium in 1997

w: A historic timber chalet in the Zakopane style, Villa Atma houses the Karol Szymanowski Museum, a department of the National Museum in Krakow dedicated to the composer who once lived here. Step inside one of the highland-style villas that define the town's architecture while learning its music history.
s: Composer Szymanowski's chalet, now a museum
_facts: Historic chalet housing the Karol Szymanowski Museum
Department of the National Museum in Krakow

w: Zakopane's main branch of the Tatra Museum gathers the history, culture, nature and ethnography of the Polish Tatras into one institution - highlander tradition, natural history and the mountaineering lore that built the town's identity. It explains why Zakopane looks the way it does before you head back to the peaks.
s: The Tatras' history, culture and nature under one roof
_facts: Museum of history, culture, nature and ethnography of the Polish Tatras
Main branch located in Zakopane

w: Beneath Malolaczniak in the Western Tatras runs Jaskinia Wielka Sniezna, the great snowy cave, a limestone labyrinth stretching 23.7 kilometres with a vertical range of 824 metres - the longest and deepest cave system in Poland. It lies within Tatra National Park and is serious caving territory, not a casual walk-in.
_facts: 23.723 km long, 824m vertical range
Longest, largest and deepest cave in Poland
Located within Tatra National Park, in Mount Malolaczniak

w: Swinica's 2,302-metre summit sits on the Polish-Slovak border along the High Tatras' main ridge, its Polish name apparently a nod to its swine-like silhouette, or, by another account, to how treacherous the climb is. First summited in 1867, the mountain's long record of fatal accidents backs up that second theory.
s: A notoriously dangerous High Tatras peak
_facts: 2,302m summit on the Polish-Slovak border
First summited by Maciej Sieczka in 1867
Name may reference resemblance to a swine, or the mountain's danger; many fatal accidents recorded

w: Four grassy, domed summits along the Western Tatras' main ridge make up Czerwone Wierchy, the Red Peaks - a name that has nothing to do with their limestone and dolomite rock. It comes from the rush Juncus trifidus blanketing the slopes, which turns red every autumn. The massif hides Poland's longest cave.
s: The 'Red Peaks' named for autumn rushes, not rock
_facts: Group of four peaks on the Western Tatras' main ridge
Name derives from the rush Juncus trifidus, which turns red in autumn
Massif contains Jaskinia Wielka Sniezna, Poland's longest cave

w: Exposed limestone cliffs on this 1,206-metre peak above Zakopane's Bystra and Olczyska valleys resemble a protruding nose, which is exactly how Nosal got its name. It has long doubled as a local training ground for skiing and paragliding, close enough to town to be Zakopane's easy answer to the bigger peaks.
s: A mountain shaped like a nose, and skied like one too
_facts: 1,206m peak above Bystra and Olczyska valleys, next to Zakopane
Name derives from nose-shaped exposed limestone rocks
Known as a place for skiing and gliding

w: At 2,291 metres, Kozi Wierch is the tallest summit located wholly inside Poland, rising between the Gasienicowa Valley and the Valley of Five Polish Lakes. It also marks the high point of Orla Perc, generally considered the most dangerous and demanding trail in the entire Tatra range.
s: The highest peak entirely within Poland's borders
_facts: 2,291m, highest peak located entirely within Poland
Highest point of the Orla Perc trail
Orla Perc considered one of the most dangerous, difficult Tatra trails
